subject: Biology
description: Excretory system, structural unit, urine formation, dialysis, common disorders

questions.stem: The structural and functional unit of the kidney is the:
questions.explanation: Nephron — basic functional unit. Each kidney has ~1 million nephrons. Components: Glomerulus (capillary tuft for filtration), Bowman's capsule, Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT, ~65% reabsorption), Loop of Henle (concentration), Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT), Collecting Duct. Glomerulus is INSIDE the nephron, not the whole nephron. Alveolus — air sac in lungs. Neuron — nerve cell.
questions.diagram_hint: Cross-section of nephron showing glomerulus inside Bowman's capsule, PCT, descending and ascending loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct, with afferent and efferent arterioles.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Filtration of blood in the nephron primarily occurs at the:

options.option_text: Glomerulus (under high hydrostatic pressure into Bowman's capsule)

questions.explanation: Glomerular Filtration — afferent arteriole brings blood at high pressure → glomerular capillaries (with fenestrated endothelium + basement membrane + podocytes) filter water + solutes → 'glomerular filtrate' enters Bowman's capsule. ~180 L/day filtered, but ~178.5 L reabsorbed downstream → only ~1.5 L excreted as urine. Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) — clinical marker of kidney function (normal ~120 mL/min).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The hormone that increases water reabsorption in the kidney's collecting duct is:
questions.explanation: ADH (Vasopressin) — secreted by posterior pituitary in response to dehydration / high blood osmolarity. Inserts aquaporin water channels into collecting duct cells → water reabsorption ↑ → urine becomes concentrated (low volume). Diabetes insipidus = ADH deficiency → very dilute, voluminous urine (polyuria). Aldosterone (adrenal cortex) increases Na⁺ reabsorption (and thereby water). RAAS (Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System) — major BP/volume regulator. Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) — opposite of aldosterone.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Approximately how much urine does a normal adult produce per day?
questions.explanation: Normal urine output: ~1-2 L/day (depends on fluid intake, climate, exercise). Composition: 95% water, 2% urea, electrolytes (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, PO₄³⁻), creatinine, urobilin (yellow colour). pH 4.5-8 (slightly acidic). Anuria (<100 mL/day) = severe kidney failure. Polyuria (>3 L/day) — often diabetes mellitus or insipidus. Oliguria (<400 mL/day) — kidney injury, dehydration.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: The yellow colour of urine is mainly due to a pigment called:
questions.explanation: Urochrome / urobilin — breakdown product of haemoglobin (RBC degradation → biliverdin → bilirubin → urobilinogen → urobilin). Bilirubin is processed by liver, conjugated, excreted in bile → broken to urobilinogen by gut bacteria → some reabsorbed and excreted in urine. High bilirubin in blood → jaundice (yellow skin/eyes). Brown urine could indicate liver issues; red could be blood (haematuria); 'tea-coloured' could suggest rhabdomyolysis (myoglobin).
questions.subject: Biology

options.option_text: Filtering waste products from blood when kidneys fail (artificial kidney)

questions.explanation: Haemodialysis — patient's blood is pumped through a semi-permeable membrane bathed in dialysate fluid. Wastes (urea, creatinine) and excess water diffuse out → cleansed blood returned. Done 3-4 times a week, ~4 hr per session. Required when kidneys lose >85% of function. Peritoneal dialysis — uses peritoneal membrane (abdominal cavity) instead of an external machine. Kidney transplantation is the definitive cure for end-stage renal disease.

questions.stem: The journey of urine from kidney to outside the body passes through (in order):
questions.explanation: Kidney → URETER (a tube ~25 cm) → URINARY BLADDER (storage, ~400-600 mL capacity) → URETHRA (a single tube to exterior; ~4 cm in females, ~20 cm in males). Two ureters (one from each kidney) drain into the bladder. Internal urethral sphincter is involuntary (smooth muscle); external urethral sphincter is voluntary (skeletal muscle) — toilet training masters this.
